definitions.definition: One of the seven (or nine) realities whose true understanding and acceptance is right view (TS 1.2, 1.4).
In Jain usage the nine categories (nava padārtha): the seven realities plus merit and demerit (Kundakunda, Śvetāmbara canon).

The soul: an eternal, formless, conscious substance whose mark is cognitive activity (upayoga), agent and enjoyer of its karma, co-extensive with its body, innumerable in number, each distinct; worldly or liberated (TS 2.8, 2.10, 5.3, 5.16).
Everything without consciousness: matter, the media of motion and rest, space and time (TS 5.1–3, 5.39).
The influx of karmic matter into the soul through the activity (yoga) of body, speech and mind (TS 6.1–2).

cross_language.note: Pali has āsava 'canker, outflow' — same word, different doctrine

definitions.definition: The binding of karmic matter with the soul because of the passions, in four aspects: nature, duration, intensity and quantity (TS 8.2–3).
The blocking of inflow, achieved by the controls, carefulnesses, virtues, reflections, endurance of hardships and conduct (TS 9.1–2).
The falling away of bound karma, either on fruition (savipāka) or before its time through austerity (avipāka) (TS 8.23, 9.3).

Release from all karma through the absence of the causes of bondage and through shedding; the liberated soul rises to the summit of the universe and abides in infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy (TS 10.2–5).
The soul's resting in its own pure nature, known already by the ultimate standpoint; the self conquered by passions is saṃsāra, the self that conquers them is liberation (YŚ 4.5).
Auspicious karma — pleasant feeling and auspicious lifespan, body-making and status (TS 8.25); in the ultimate view merit too is a fetter, 'a golden chain' (Kundakunda).
Inauspicious karma (TS 8.26); also the five sins — violence, falsehood, theft, unchastity, possessiveness.
Right view, right knowledge and right conduct, which together are the path to liberation (TS 1.1); in the ultimate sense they are the self itself (YŚ 4.2; Yogaśataka 2).
Conviction in the realities as they are (TS 1.2); arising naturally or through instruction; by the ultimate standpoint, the direct experience of the pure self (Samayasāra 11).
Knowledge of the realities free of doubt, error and indefiniteness; the five knowledges when accompanied by right view.
Abstention from the causes of inflow — vows, carefulness, restraint — undertaken on the basis of right view and knowledge; ultimately, abiding in the self.
The single path constituted by the three jewels together (TS 1.1).

The state of right view, with its eight limbs (freedom from doubt, from desire, from disgust, from delusion; upholding, stabilising, affection, illuminating the teaching), its signs (calm, longing for release, detachment, compassion, affirmation) and its kinds (subsidential, mixed, destructional).
Right view arising spontaneously, from the soul's own purification, without instruction in this life (TS 1.3).
Right view arising through instruction or study (TS 1.3); also 'understanding' of the realities through pramāṇa and naya (TS 1.6).
The fourfold setting of a word's reference — by name, representation (image), potentiality (dravya) and actuality (bhāva) — to avoid confusion (TS 1.5).

Six substances make up the universe — soul, matter, the media of motion and rest, space and time; a substance is the existent, endowed with origination, cessation and persistence, and possesses qualities and modes (TS 5.2, 5.29–30, 5.38). Also, in nikṣepa, 'potentiality'.
The five substances that exist with extension in space-points — soul, matter, medium of motion, medium of rest, space (time excluded) (TS 5.1; Kundakunda's Pañcāstikāya).

A single, formless, world-pervading substance that assists (without causing) the motion of souls and matter, as water assists fish (TS 5.17); its absence beyond the world stops the liberated soul at the summit (TS 10.8).
A single, formless, world-pervading substance that assists the rest of moving things, as shade assists a traveller (TS 5.17).
The substance that gives room to all others; divided into world-space (lokākāśa), where the other substances are, and infinite empty non-world space (alokākāśa) (TS 5.9, 5.12, 5.18).
The finite portion of space occupied by the other substances — the universe (TS 5.12).

The only substance with form: atoms and aggregates having touch, taste, smell and colour, taking the forms of sound, darkness, light and bodies; karma itself is a subtle kind of matter (TS 5.5, 5.23–28, 8.2).

cross_language.note: Pali puggala means 'person' — a different sense

definitions.definition: The partless unit of matter, occupying one space-point, with one taste, colour, smell and two touches; atoms bind by degrees of smoothness and roughness (TS 5.25–37).
In Jain usage a molecule or compound of atoms, formed by union and division; visible bodies are aggregates (TS 5.25–28).

The substance that makes possible continuity, change, activity and priority (TS 5.22); for the Digambaras a real substance consisting of innumerable time-atoms, one in each space-point; for some Śvetāmbaras only a mode of other substances ('according to some', Śv 5.38). Conventional time is measured by the luminaries.
The ongoing persistence-in-change of each thing, assisted by time (TS 5.22).
The smallest indivisible unit of time — the time an atom takes to move to the adjacent space-point (TS 2.29, 5.40). Also 'doctrine' and, in the Samayasāra, 'the self'.
The unit of extension occupied by one atom; souls and the media have innumerable, space infinite (TS 5.8–11).
In Jain usage an inherent quality of a substance, present in all its modes and itself without qualities (TS 5.38, 5.41).
A changing state of a substance; modes arise and cease while the substance persists (TS 1.26, 1.29, 5.38).
What is endowed with origination, cessation and persistence (TS 5.29–30).
The triple mark of every existent (TS 5.30): a thing persists as substance while its modes arise and pass away.
The becoming of qualities and substances through their modes (TS 5.42); change within persistence.
A grouping of material particles by fineness; the karmic class (kārmaṇa-vargaṇā) is the matter drawn in and bound as karma.
The defining mark of the soul: its activity of knowing and perceiving — eight kinds of knowledge-activity and four of perception-activity (TS 2.8–9).
In Jain epistemology the indeterminate, general grasp of an object preceding knowledge (visual, non-visual, clairvoyant, omniscient); in 'samyag-darśana', view or faith; also a philosophical system.
The soul's four infinite qualities manifest on destruction of the obscuring karmas: infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy.
A state arising from the temporary subsidence of (deluding) karma — right view and conduct (TS 2.3).
A state arising from the destruction of karma — knowledge, perception, giving, gain, enjoyment, energy, right view and conduct (TS 2.4).
A state arising from partial destruction and partial subsidence of karma — most ordinary knowledge and perception (TS 2.5).
States produced by the fruition of karma: destinies, passions, sexes, wrong view, ignorance, non-restraint, non-perfection, leśyās (TS 2.6).
States belonging to the soul by its own nature, independent of karma: being a soul, capability and incapability for liberation (TS 2.7).
A soul capable of attaining liberation (TS 2.7); not every capable soul will actually attain it.
A soul that by its inherent nature will never attain liberation (TS 2.7).
A soul bound in the cycle of births (TS 2.10).
A soul freed of all karma (TS 2.10).
A soul with two to five senses, able to move of its own will (TS 2.12, 2.14).
One-sensed souls embodied in earth, water, fire, air and plants (Digambara TS 2.13; the Śvetāmbara recension counts fire and air as mobile).
A five-sensed being possessing mind (samanaska) (TS 2.11, 2.24).
In Jain analysis five senses, each twofold: physical (formation and instrument) and psychic (attainment and use) (TS 2.15–19).

In Jain usage the 'quasi-sense' (anindriya/noindriya): the physical mind (dravya-manas) is fine matter, the psychic mind (bhāva-manas) the soul's capacity; its object is scriptural knowledge (TS 1.14, 2.21, 5.19).
In Jain usage the ten vitalities of an embodied soul: the five senses, the three powers (mind, speech, body), breath and lifespan; violence is the severing of these (TS 7.13).

notes: Distinct from the yogic prāṇa (breath/vital wind) — see trm:prana-vayu-jain.

definitions.definition: One of the four states of embodied existence — hellish, animal, human, divine — determined by karma (TS 2.6, 8.11); also motion.
All beings other than gods, hell-beings and humans — one-sensed beings, insects, animals (TS 4.27).
In Jain cosmology a class of embodied beings of the four orders, born by spontaneous arising, enjoying the fruits of merit, and not liberated; gods cannot take vows or attain liberation directly.
The seven infernal earths below the middle world and their beings, who suffer by their own leśyā, one another, and (in the first three) the asuras (TS 3.1–6).
The transit of the soul between death and rebirth, with the karmic body only, along the rows of space-points, taking up to four instants (TS 2.25–30).
The state of the soul in transit for one to three instants, when it takes in no matter to build a body (TS 2.30).
The birth of gods and hell-beings, arising in a birth-place without parents (TS 2.31, 2.34).
Birth by aggregation of matter without parents, as of one-sensed and many small beings (TS 2.31, 2.35).
The physical body of humans and animals (TS 2.36).
The body of gods and hell-beings, which can change size and form; also gained by some ascetics as an attainment (TS 2.36, 2.46–47).
A subtle auspicious body projected by an advanced ascetic in the sixth stage to consult an omniscient (TS 2.36, 2.49).
A subtle luminous body of heat that accompanies every worldly soul and digests; by attainment it can be projected to burn or to bless (TS 2.36, 2.48).
The subtlest body, made of the soul's bound karma, beginninglessly connected with every worldly soul and carrying it between births (TS 2.25, 2.36, 2.40–42).
The body in which a soul will attain liberation; its lifespan cannot be cut short (TS 2.53).

(1) A power arising from the destruction-cum-subsidence of karma through austerity — e.g. the transformable or fiery body, healing powers, sky-travel (TS 2.47–48); (2) one of the nine destructional attainments of the omniscient (TS 2.4).
Knowledge through the senses and mind, including memory, recognition, reasoning and inference, in four stages (TS 1.9, 1.13–15).
Knowledge through words and signs, preceded by sensory knowledge; especially the scriptures (aṅga and outside the aṅgas) (TS 1.9, 1.20).
Direct knowledge by the soul of material things within a range, innate in gods and hell-beings and acquired by others (TS 1.21–22, 1.27).

literal: knowledge of the modes of minds

definitions.definition: Direct knowledge of the thoughts of others, only in restrained ascetics; straight or extensive (TS 1.23–25, 1.28).
Perfect knowledge of all substances in all their modes, past, present and future, arising when the knowledge-obscuring and other destructive karmas are destroyed (TS 1.29, 10.1).
The omniscient's perception of all things in their general aspect; whether it occurs in sequence with, simultaneously with, or identical to omniscient knowledge is debated.
The omniscient teacher whose existence Jain logicians defend against Mīmāṃsā (Āptamīmāṃsā 4–5).
One who has attained omniscience; the Tīrthaṅkaras are kevalins who found a teaching-ford, others are ordinary kevalins.
In Jain epistemology knowledge by the soul without senses — clairvoyance, mind-reading, omniscience (TS 1.12); later also sense-perception as 'conventionally direct' (Akalaṅka).
Knowledge through senses, mind or words — sensory and scriptural knowledge (TS 1.11); later memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and testimony.
Akalaṅka's name for sense-perception, direct only by conventional usage (Laghīyastraya).

In Jain epistemology valid knowledge itself — the five knowledges (TS 1.10); knowledge illuminating itself and its object, free from contradiction (Nyāyāvatāra 1); the right ascertainment of an object (Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.1.2).
A form of sensory (mati) knowledge (TS 1.13); in Akalaṅka's scheme an indirect pramāṇa.
Recognition ('this is that') as a form of mati (saṃjñā, TS 1.13) and, for Akalaṅka, an independent indirect pramāṇa.
In Jain logic the knowledge of invariable concomitance (cintā, TS 1.13), an independent indirect pramāṇa.
The first stage of sensory knowledge: the bare grasping of an object after contact (TS 1.15).
The second stage: the inquiring wish to know the particular (TS 1.15).
The third stage: the definite ascertainment of the particular (TS 1.15).

(1) In Jain epistemology the fourth stage of sensory knowledge: retention enabling memory (TS 1.15). (2) In Jain yoga, concentration — Haribhadra's kāntā view; Hemacandra's five visualised concentrations of embodied meditation (YŚ 7).
Wrong knowledge: sensory, scriptural and clairvoyant knowledge in one with wrong view, who does not distinguish real and unreal (TS 1.31–32).
A partial viewpoint grasping one aspect of a many-sided thing; valid when it does not deny the others, false when taken as the whole (TS 1.6, 1.33; Sanmati).
The standpoint that takes general and particular together, or speaks of a thing by its intended end (as 'I am cooking' of one gathering fuel) (TS 1.33).
The standpoint that grasps the general, uniting all things under a common character such as 'existent' (TS 1.33); taken absolutely it becomes a monism.

term: vyavahāra (the third of the seven nayas)
native: व्यवहार (थे थिर्द् ओफ़् थे सेवेन् नयस्)

definitions.definition: The third of the seven standpoints: it divides the general into particulars for practical dealings (TS 1.33); distinct from vyavahāra paired with niścaya.
The standpoint that attends only to the present mode (TS 1.33); taken absolutely it becomes the Buddhist doctrine of momentariness.
The standpoint that distinguishes meaning by grammatical features such as tense, gender and number (TS 1.33).
The standpoint that distinguishes synonyms by their etymology (TS 1.33).
The standpoint that applies a word only when the thing is actually performing the action the word names — Indra only while ruling (TS 1.33).
The root standpoint that looks to the enduring substance (Sanmati 1.3).
The root standpoint that looks to the changing modes (Sanmati 1.3).
The ultimate standpoint, which views the soul in its own pure nature, unbound and unconnected with matter (Samayasāra 11, 14); said to be the real (bhūtārtha).
For the Adhyātma movement the standpoint of one's own pure self, known in self-experience; the refuge of right view, to be held together with vyavahāra (Samayasāra Nāṭaka).

The conventional standpoint, which describes the soul through its relations with karma, body and practice; needed to teach the ultimate as a foreign tongue is needed to teach a foreigner (Samayasāra 8), but called unreal (abhūtārtha) (Samayasāra 11).
Outward conduct, ritual and the stages of practice — valid in their place, but not to be mistaken for the self (Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka).
What is described by the ultimate standpoint (Samayasāra 11; Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 5).
What the conventional standpoint describes — not false, but not the thing's own nature (Samayasāra 11).
The doctrine that reality has infinite aspects (e.g. permanent as substance, impermanent as modes), so that every statement is true only in some respect (TS 5.30–32; Āptamīmāṃsā).
The method of qualifying every predication with 'syāt' (in some respect) to express many-sidedness (Āptamīmāṃsā 104–105).

The seven possible predications about any attribute: in some respect it is; is not; is and is not; is inexpressible; is and is inexpressible; is not and is inexpressible; is, is not and is inexpressible (Āptamīmāṃsā 14).
The particle marking the conditional, respect-bound nature of a predication — not doubt but 'from a certain standpoint' (kathaṃcit).
The fourth predication: a thing as simultaneously existent and non-existent cannot be expressed in one word.
An absolutist view that takes one aspect for the whole; the root of all rival doctrines in the Jain analysis.
A statement presenting the whole thing through one attribute, belonging to pramāṇa (Rājavārttika 1.6).
A statement presenting one aspect only, belonging to naya (Rājavārttika 1.6).

literal: other doctrine; the self in the other

definitions.definition: (1) A rival doctrine — as many as the standpoints (Sanmati 3.47); (2) in the Samayasāra, the soul dwelling in the non-self (karma, body), opposed to sva-samaya, the soul in its own nature.

Subtle matter drawn into the soul by its activity and bound by its passions, veiling its qualities and producing its states until shed (TS 8.2); 'material karma' (dravya-karma) as distinct from the soul's passional states (bhāva-karma).

(1) In Jain karma theory the vibration or activity of body, speech and mind which is the channel of inflow (TS 6.1–2); (2) in Jain yoga texts, whatever joins the soul to liberation — the three jewels (YŚ 1.15; Yogaviṃśikā 1).
Inflow of one with passions, producing bondage of duration (TS 6.4).
Inflow of one without passions (stages 11–13), which does not stay bound beyond an instant (TS 6.4).
The kind of karma bound — which of the eight types (TS 8.3–4).
How long the bound karma remains before fruition (TS 8.14–20).
The strength of the karma's fruition, depending on the intensity of passion (TS 8.21–22).
The mass of karmic particles bound to the soul's space-points, depending on activity (TS 8.24).
The four karmas that obscure the soul's own qualities — knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, deluding and obstructive; their destruction yields omniscience (TS 10.1).
Karma veiling the five kinds of knowledge (TS 8.4, 8.6).
Karma veiling perception and producing the five kinds of sleep (TS 8.7).
Karma producing pleasant and unpleasant feeling (TS 8.8).
The chief karma, deluding view and conduct; its destruction comes first on the way to omniscience (TS 8.9, 10.1).
The three karmas deluding view: wrong view, mixed, and the 'right-view' karma that allows a clouded right view (TS 8.9).
The twenty-five karmas deluding conduct: sixteen passions and nine quasi-passions (TS 8.9).
Karma fixing the lifespan in one of four destinies; bound once in a life (TS 8.10).
Karma determining destiny, class, body, form, and all bodily particulars, including Tīrthaṅkarahood (TS 8.11).
Karma determining high or low status (TS 8.12, 6.25–26).
Karma obstructing giving, gain, enjoyment and energy (TS 8.13, 6.27).
The auspicious body-making karma that makes a soul a founder of the teaching-ford, bound through sixteen causes (TS 6.24, 8.11).
The four passions — anger, pride, deceit, greed — which make karma stick to the soul (TS 6.4, 8.2); each in four grades of intensity.
In Jain usage the passion of deceit or crookedness, cause of animal rebirth (TS 6.16) and one of the three thorns.

notes: Distinct from the Advaita māyā (cosmic appearance).

definitions.definition: The most intense grade of the passions, which obstructs right view and binds to endless rebirth (TS 8.9).
The grade of passions that prevents taking even the lay vows (TS 8.9).
The grade of passions that prevents the great vows (TS 8.9).
The subtlest grade of passions, which remains even in the monk and blocks perfect conduct (TS 8.9).
The nine passion-like emotions: laughter, liking, disliking, grief, fear, disgust and the three sexual drives (TS 8.9).

The coloration of the soul by passion-tinged activity, in six grades — black, blue, grey (inauspicious), yellow-red, lotus-pink, white (auspicious); physical (dravya) and psychic (bhāva) (TS 2.6; Uttarādhyayana 34).
Wrong view — the first cause of bondage (TS 8.1); five kinds in the Digambara list (one-sided, contrary, indiscriminate reverence, doubtful, ignorant).
In Jain usage the lack of renunciation of violence and the other sins — the second cause of bondage (TS 8.1).

equivalents.note: Yoga Sūtra 1.30 avirati is craving for sense objects; the Jain term is non-renunciation of the five sins.

definitions.definition: In Jain usage heedlessness in conduct (fifteen kinds in Digambara analysis: gossip, passions, senses, sleep, affection) — the cause that makes killing 'violence' (TS 7.13, 8.1).

equivalents.note: Yoga Sūtra 1.30 pramāda is neglect of the means of samādhi; the Jain term is broader heedlessness of conduct.

definitions.definition: In Jain usage the experiencing of karma's fruit according to its nature, after which it is shed (TS 8.21–23).
The projection of the soul's space-points beyond the body without leaving it — at death, in pain, passion, or (for the kevalin) to equalise the remaining karmas before liberation.
The finite universe of the six substances within infinite empty space, shaped like a standing man (loka-puruṣa), uncreated and beginningless.
Infinite empty space beyond the universe, into which nothing can move since the medium of motion is absent (TS 10.8).
The universe pictured as a man standing with arms akimbo: the lower world as legs, the middle world at the waist, the heavens as chest and head, the abode of the liberated at the crown.
The seven hellish earths (TS 3.1).
The disc of concentric continents and oceans around Jambūdvīpa, where humans and animals live (TS 3.7–9).
The heavens of the celestial-vehicle gods, rising to the Sarvārthasiddhi vehicle, above which is the abode of the liberated.
The crescent-shaped region (īṣatprāgbhārā) at the summit of the universe, above which the liberated souls abide.
The central vertical column of the universe, one rajju wide, outside which mobile beings do not live.
The central, round continent of the middle world, 100,000 yojanas across, with Meru at its centre (TS 3.9).
The first ocean ringing Jambūdvīpa (TS 3.7).
The mountain at the navel of Jambūdvīpa, around which the luminaries turn (TS 3.9, 4.13).
The ring-mountain in Puṣkaradvīpa marking the limit of the human world of two and a half continents (TS 3.35).
The southern region of Jambūdvīpa, our world, subject to the ascending and descending time cycles (TS 3.10, 3.27).
The central region of Jambūdvīpa where time does not cycle and Tīrthaṅkaras (such as Sīmandhara) teach now (TS 3.10, 3.31).
Regions where people live by work, where religious practice and liberation are possible and Tīrthaṅkaras arise (TS 3.37).
Regions where wish-fulfilling trees provide all needs, lifespans are long and liberation is not possible (TS 3.28–31).
The half of the time-wheel in which happiness, lifespan and virtue decline through six periods; the present age is its fifth period (TS 3.27).
The half of the time-wheel in which conditions improve through six periods (TS 3.27).
One of the six periods of each half-cycle: very happy, happy, happy-unhappy, unhappy-happy, unhappy, very unhappy (suṣama-suṣamā … duṣama-duṣamā).
A vast unit of time measured by emptying a pit filled with fine hairs, one per century (TS 3.29, 3.38).
Ten koṭākoṭi palyopamas; used for the lifespans of gods and hell-beings and for karmic durations (TS 3.6, 8.14).
Any interval less than 48 minutes — the maximum span of one meditation (TS 9.27).
The first order of gods, living in mansions in the upper layer of the first earth: asura, nāga and other 'princes' (TS 4.10).
The second order of gods — kinnaras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas and others (TS 4.11).
The third order of gods: sun, moon, planets, lunar mansions and stars, whose motion around Meru measures time (TS 4.12–15).
The fourth order, dwelling in heavens one above another (TS 4.16–19).
Vaimānika gods of the kalpa heavens, with ranks such as Indra (16 heavens for Digambaras, 12 for Śvetāmbaras) (TS 4.17, 4.19).
Vaimānika gods above the kalpas — the Graiveyakas and Anuttaras — without ranks, all equal ('ahamindra') (TS 4.17).
The nine heavens at the 'neck' of the cosmic person (TS 4.19).
The five highest heavens (Vijaya, Vaijayanta, Jayanta, Aparājita, Sarvārthasiddhi), whose gods are near liberation (TS 4.19, 4.26).
Gods of the Brahmaloka who, being near liberation, come to urge each Tīrthaṅkara to renounce (TS 4.24–25).
Abstention from violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and possessiveness — partial for the householder, complete for the ascetic (TS 7.1–2).
In Jainism the five vows taken in full by ascetics, to be kept in thought, word and deed, doing, causing and approving (TS 7.2).
The five vows kept partially by the householder (TS 7.2, 7.20).

The first and chief vow: not severing the vitalities of any being through careless (passion-driven) activity (TS 7.13); inwardly, the non-arising of attachment and other passions (Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 44); called the supreme Brahman (Svayambhūstotra).
The severing of life-forces through careless activity (TS 7.13); twofold — material (dravya) and psychic (bhāva, the passion itself) (Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya).
In Jainism abstention from saying what is not good (asat) — false, harsh or harmful (TS 7.14); also a tenfold virtue (9.6).
In Jainism abstention from taking what is not given (TS 7.15).
In Jainism abstention from sexual activity (complete for ascetics, limited to one's spouse for laity) (TS 7.16); also the last of the ten virtues.
In Jainism abstention from possessiveness, defined as infatuation (mūrcchā) (TS 7.17).
Infatuation with things (TS 7.17); external (ten kinds of property) and internal (fourteen: wrong view, passions, quasi-passions).
The inner attachment that constitutes possessiveness, whether or not one owns anything (TS 7.17).
Three lay vows strengthening the small vows — commonly limiting direction, purposeless harm, and consumables (lists differ by author).
Four lay vows of training in ascetic practice — commonly sāmāyika, limiting region, fasting on holy days and sharing with guests (lists differ).
Lifelong limitation of the distance one will travel in each direction (TS 7.21).
Temporary further restriction of the area of one's activity (TS 7.21).
Avoiding harmful acts without purpose — evil counsel, careless acts, giving weapons, harmful thoughts and entertainments (TS 7.21).
Limiting things used once (food) and things used repeatedly (clothes, dwellings) (TS 7.21).

The practice of sitting in equanimity, renouncing all harmful activity for a fixed period (commonly 48 minutes); a lay vow (TS 7.21), the first of the five conducts (TS 9.18) and the first of the six essential duties.
Fasting and spending the eighth and fourteenth days of the fortnight in religious practice as a temporary ascetic (TS 7.21); Śvetāmbara pauṣadha.
Giving pure food and requisites to ascetics who come unannounced (TS 7.21).
Relinquishing what is one's own for the benefit of self and other; its merit depends on manner, gift, giver and recipient (TS 7.38–39); four kinds — food, medicine, knowledge, fearlessness.
A householder with the thirty-five preliminary virtues (honest wealth and the rest) that prepare for the vows (YŚ 1.47–56; Dharmabindu).
For laity, eight basic observances (abstaining from wine, meat, honey and certain fruits, or with the small vows); for Digambara monks, twenty-eight basic qualities (Mūlācāra).
A partial lapse in a vow or in right view, five for each (TS 7.23–37).
The three thorns that disqualify a vow-holder: deceit, longing for future reward, and wrong view (TS 7.18).
The wish that one's austerities bring a particular worldly or heavenly reward; a thorn, a form of sorrowful meditation and a fault of sallekhanā (TS 7.37, 9.33).

The voluntary, gradual giving up of food and passions when death is inevitable, undertaken without passion, with the teacher's permission (TS 7.22; Ratnakaraṇḍa 122); held by the tradition not to be self-killing.

notes: Restricted topic: see cpt:sallekhana and prc:sallekhana (summary and the texts' own conditions only).

definitions.definition: Śvetāmbara vernacular name for the fast unto death undertaken at the end of life.
Dying with a composed, detached mind absorbed in the self and the recitation of the Jina's name; the aim of sallekhanā.
The death of a restrained ascetic by renunciation of food in equanimity (Bhagavatī Ārādhanā).
The death of one without vows (or without right view), with attachment and fear.
An attending ascetic who guides and strengthens the one undertaking the final fast (Bhagavatī Ārādhanā).

In Jainism (1) the five contemplations supporting each vow (TS 7.3–8); (2) the twelve reflections (anuprekṣā); (3) the four attitudes of friendliness and the rest; (4) in Haribhadra's Yogabindu, the second of five yogas.
In Jainism friendliness toward all beings — 'may no one do evil, may no one suffer, may the world be freed' (TS 7.11; YŚ 4.118).
Delight at the qualities of those more virtuous (TS 7.11); Jain counterpart of muditā.
In Jainism compassion toward the afflicted (TS 7.11: kāruṇya).
(1) Equanimity toward the unruly and incorrigible (TS 7.11); (2) impartiality of mind between doctrines, following reason (Jñānasāra 16; Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 8).
In Jainism fear of worldly existence and longing for liberation, one of the signs of right view (TS 7.12, 6.24).
In Jainism detachment cultivated by contemplating the world and the body (TS 7.12); threefold — born of suffering, of delusion and of knowledge, only the last true (Adhyātmasāra).
'Souls render service to one another' (TS 5.21) — the function of souls toward each other; now a motto of the Jain community.
Samantabhadra's name for the Jina's teaching as leading all to welfare (Yuktyanuśāsana).
Proper restraint of the activity of mind, speech and body (TS 9.4) — three controls.
Careful conduct in walking, speaking, seeking alms, handling objects and excreting, so as to harm no being (TS 9.5).
The eight 'mothers' — five carefulnesses and three controls — from which all monastic conduct is born (Uttarādhyayana 24).
The first of the ten virtues: forgiveness and patience under provocation (TS 9.6).
The second virtue: freedom from pride (TS 9.6).
The third virtue: freedom from deceit (TS 9.6).
In Jainism the fourth virtue: purity from greed (TS 9.6).
The sixth virtue: restraint of senses and protection of beings (TS 9.6); also self-discipline generally.
The eighth virtue: giving up, including giving knowledge and other gifts (TS 9.6).
The ninth virtue: the attitude 'nothing is mine' (TS 9.6).

In Jainism (1) the medium of motion (dharmāstikāya); (2) the tenfold virtue beginning with forbearance (TS 9.6); (3) the three jewels; (4) the nature of a thing and the protection of beings (Kārttikeyānuprekṣā 478).

Repeated contemplation of twelve themes — impermanence, no refuge, the round of births, aloneness, otherness, impurity, inflow, stopping, shedding, the universe, rarity of enlightenment, and the well-taught dharma (TS 9.7); also a kind of study (9.25).
The eleventh reflection: how rare right view, knowledge and conduct are among all births (TS 9.7).
One of twenty-two afflictions (hunger, thirst, cold, heat, nakedness, abuse, and the rest) to be endured without swerving from the path (TS 9.8–9).
Enduring the hardships calmly, a means of stopping and shedding karma (TS 9.2, 9.8).
Right conduct, of five kinds — equanimity, re-initiation, special purificatory austerity, subtle passion, perfect conduct (TS 9.18).
Perfect conduct of the passionless (stages 11–14) (TS 9.18).

In Jainism twelvefold — six external (fasting, eating less, restricting alms, giving up tasty food, lonely seat, bodily mortification) and six internal (expiation, humility, service, study, abandonment, meditation) — which both stops and sheds karma (TS 9.3, 9.19–20).
The six outwardly visible austerities (TS 9.19).
The six inner austerities culminating in meditation (TS 9.20).
Abstaining from food for a fixed period or, at life's end, until death (TS 9.19).
Eating less than one's fill (Śvetāmbara ūnodarī) (TS 9.19).
Accepting alms only under self-set conditions (TS 9.19).
Abstaining from rich or savoury foods (ghee, milk, sweets, salt) (TS 9.19).
Dwelling and sitting in secluded places free of disturbance (TS 9.19); Śvetāmbara saṃlīnatā.
Enduring bodily hardship — difficult postures, exposure — in the list of external austerities (TS 9.19).
Nine (Śvetāmbara ten) forms of correcting a fault, from confession to re-initiation (TS 9.22).
Disclosing one's faults to the teacher without concealment (TS 9.22).
Reviewing and repenting of faults committed — an expiation (TS 9.22) and one of the six essential duties, performed daily, fortnightly, four-monthly and yearly.
A formal resolve to give up something (food, activities) for a period; one of the six essential duties.
Formal veneration of the teacher; one of the six essential duties.
Praise of the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras (the Logassa hymn); one of the six essential duties.
Standing (or sitting) motionless, indifferent to the body, for a set period measured in recitations; an essential duty and a form of internal austerity (vyutsarga).
Giving up external and internal attachments, including the body (TS 9.20, 9.26).

The six obligatory daily practices: equanimity, praise of the twenty-four, salutation, repentance, body-abandonment and renunciation (for householders the Digambaras also teach six daily duties: worship, service of the teacher, study, restraint, austerity, giving).
Reverence toward knowledge, view, conduct and the worthy (TS 9.23).
Service to teachers, ascetics, novices, the sick and the community (TS 9.24).
In Jainism fivefold: reading/teaching, questioning, reflection, recitation and preaching (TS 9.25).
Mutual asking and granting of forgiveness, above all at the end of Paryuṣaṇa ('micchāmi dukkaḍaṃ').
The Prakrit formula of repentance and request for forgiveness spoken in pratikramaṇa and at Paryuṣaṇa.
One of the eleven stages of lay renunciation, from right view to not accepting food prepared for oneself (Ratnakaraṇḍa); also a statue.
The Jain householder who hears the teaching and keeps the small vows (TS 7.19–20).
In Jainism the homeless ascetic under the great vows.
A Jain monk (sādhvī, nun), the fifth of the supreme beings honoured in the Namaskāra mantra.
The Jain ascetic, free of outer and inner attachments; five kinds (TS 9.46); the early name of Jain mendicants.
The ascetic's periodic plucking out of the hair of head and face by hand, at initiation and thereafter.
The strongest joint-structure of the body, required for meditation of the highest kind (TS 9.27); held to be unavailable in the present age.

In Jainism the stopping of the mind's wandering by fixing it on one object, for up to a muhūrta (TS 9.27); fourfold — sorrowful, cruel, virtuous, pure (9.28), only the last two leading to liberation; 'a steady mind is dhyāna' (Dhyānaśataka).
The definition of meditation in TS 9.27.
Brooding on getting rid of the disagreeable, keeping the agreeable, removing pain, and future rewards (TS 9.30–33).
Delighting in violence, falsehood, theft and guarding one's possessions (TS 9.35).
Meditation examining the Jina's command, the harm of wrong ways, the fruition of karma and the structure of the universe (TS 9.36); leads to heaven and toward liberation.
The highest meditation in four stages, the first two for knowers of the Pūrvas, the last two for the omniscient, ending in liberation (TS 9.37–44).
Contemplating reality as taught by the Jina (TS 9.36).
Contemplating the misery of beings caught in wrong views and how they may be freed (TS 9.36).
Contemplating how the karmas bear fruit (TS 9.36).
Contemplating the shape and constitution of the universe (TS 9.36).
The first pure meditation: scripture-based contemplation shifting among aspects, words and activities of a substance (TS 9.39–44).

literal: with unity and reasoning, without shifting

definitions.definition: The second pure meditation: fixed on one aspect without shifting; it destroys the remaining destructive karmas and yields omniscience (TS 9.39, 9.42).
The third pure meditation of the omniscient, in which only subtle bodily activity remains (TS 9.39–40).
The fourth pure meditation, with all activity stopped, just before liberation (TS 9.39–40); also called samucchinna-kriyā.
In Jain meditation theory vitarka is scriptural knowledge (śruta) (TS 9.43).
In Jain meditation theory (TS spelling vīcāra) the moving between object, word and activity (TS 9.44).
The qualified meditator described in the Jñānārṇava and Yogaśāstra (detached, steady in vows, free of passion).
Meditation on the embodied self through the five visualised concentrations (YŚ 7.8–28; Jñānārṇava).
Meditation on sacred syllables, letters and mantras (YŚ 8).
Meditation on the Arhat's form in the assembly hall (YŚ 9).
Meditation on the formless, blissful Siddha (YŚ 10.1).
First of the five concentrations: visualising the middle world as an ocean of milk with a golden lotus and oneself on it (YŚ 7).
Visualising fire rising from the syllable 'arhaṃ' and burning the lotus of the eight karmas and the body (YŚ 7).
Visualising a wind that scatters the ashes (YŚ 7).
Visualising rain that washes away the remaining ash (YŚ 7).
The fifth concentration: seeing oneself as the pure, omniscient self, like a Siddha (YŚ 7).
In Hemacandra's scheme the first, restless state of mind (YŚ 12.2).
The second state of mind, sometimes still, sometimes wandering, with some bliss (YŚ 12.2–3).
The third, steady and blissful state of mind (YŚ 12.2–4).
The fourth, very steady state of mind with highest bliss (YŚ 12.2–4).
The state beyond mind described by Hemacandra from experience, reached by effortless indifference (YŚ 12).
Letting the mind alone without forcing it — Hemacandra's key to stillness (YŚ 12).
The equal-mindedness that is both cause and fruit of meditation (YŚ 4.114); the essence of sāmāyika.
Foreknowing the time of death by signs in breath, body and dreams (YŚ 5).
In Hemacandra's account the five winds (prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna) with their colours and seats, and the breath's four circles — described but not made a means to liberation (YŚ 5).
Entry into another's body, described by Hemacandra as a mere wonder of no use for liberation (YŚ 5–6.1).
In Jainism an effect of perception-obscuring karma, in five grades from light sleep to somnambulism (TS 8.7).

One of fourteen stages of the soul's purification from wrong view to the omniscient without activity, defined by the rise, subsidence and destruction of deluding and other karmas (Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama; Sarvārthasiddhi 1.8; Gommaṭasāra).
The first guṇasthāna: wrong view under the rise of view-deluding karma.
The second guṇasthāna: a momentary state while falling from right view, retaining a trace of its taste.
The third guṇasthāna: a mixture of right and wrong view.
The fourth guṇasthāna: right view attained but no vows yet taken.
The fifth guṇasthāna: the layman with the small vows.
The sixth guṇasthāna: the ascetic under the great vows with residual carelessness.
The seventh guṇasthāna: restraint free of carelessness, alternating with the sixth.
The eighth guṇasthāna (nivṛtti-bādara), where the ascetic mounts the ladder of subsidence or destruction; also the second of the three karaṇas before right view.
The ninth guṇasthāna, where gross passions are subsided or destroyed.
The tenth guṇasthāna: only subtle greed remains.
The eleventh guṇasthāna: delusion wholly subsided but not destroyed — one falls back from here.
The twelfth guṇasthāna: delusion destroyed; the other destructive karmas follow, yielding omniscience.
The thirteenth guṇasthāna: the living omniscient, teaching and moving until the end of life.
The fourteenth guṇasthāna: all activity stopped, lasting the time to utter five short syllables before liberation.
The ascent (stages 8–11) by suppressing the deluding karma, from which the soul falls back.
The ascent (stages 8–10, 12) by destroying the deluding karma, leading without fall to omniscience.
The first of three processes by which a soul approaches right view, reducing karmic durations to the 'knot'.
The third process, after which right view arises (granthi-bheda).
The breaking of the dense knot of attachment and aversion, at which right view first arises; Haribhadra places it at the sthirā view.
One of Haribhadra's eight stages of yogic vision, marked by growing clarity of understanding (YDS 13).
First view: dim, like a straw-fire spark; restraint (yama); no fatigue; non-aversion (YDS).
Second view: like cow-dung fire; observance (niyama); no anxiety; desire to know (YDS).
Third view: like wood fire; posture; no distraction; desire to hear (YDS).
Fourth view: like a lamp; breath-control (inner sense); no agitation; hearing (YDS).
Fifth view: like a gem; the knot broken and right view arisen; sense-withdrawal; understanding (YDS).
Sixth view: like a star; concentration; no delight in other; reflection (YDS).
Seventh view: like the sun; meditation; action without attachment (YDS).
Eighth view: like the moon; absorption; omniscience and liberation (YDS).
The ordinary view of beings carried along by the stream of worldly existence, contrasted with the yoga views (YDS).
Practice by one who wishes to practise but is careless (YDS).
Diligent practice following the scriptures (YDS).
Yoga beyond the scope of scripture, by one's own power; of two kinds, renunciation of dharmas and renunciation of yoga (YDS).
The capacity-yoga in which the qualities arising from destruction-cum-subsidence are given up (at the second apūrvakaraṇa) (YDS).
The final capacity-yoga in which all activity (yoga) is abandoned, at the end of the omniscient's life (YDS).
Religious activity that flows spontaneously without attachment, in the prabhā view; Haribhadra says others call it praśāntavāhitā, visabhāga-parikṣaya, śivavartman and dhruvādhvan (YDS).

equivalents.note: Equivalence asserted by Haribhadra himself; Pātañjala commentators do not make it.

definitions.definition: (1) In Haribhadra's Yogabindu the first yoga: study and contemplation of reality with friendliness etc. by one with vows; (2) in Yaśovijaya, pure activity centred on the self by one free of delusion (Adhyātmasāra 1.2); (3) the name of the seventeenth-century movement centred on the Samayasāra.
The study and direct experience of the pure self (śuddhātman) by the ultimate standpoint, as taught in the Samayasāra and its Hindi renderings.
The fourth yoga of the Yogabindu: seeing the agreeable and disagreeable as equal, not grasping at powers.
The fifth yoga of the Yogabindu: the cessation at the root of activities born of body and mind, leading to omniscience and liberation.
In the Yogaviṃśikā the fourth yoga: meditation with an external support such as the Jina's image.
The fifth yoga of the Yogaviṃśikā: meditation on the formless Siddha, leading to omniscience.

literal: one who will not again bind [the maximum]

definitions.definition: A soul that will never again bind karma of the maximum duration — the first qualification for yoga (Yogabindu).
The last cycle of matter-transformation (pudgala-parāvarta) before liberation, in which alone yoga takes hold (Yogabindu, Yogaviṃśikā).
The preliminaries to yoga: worship of teachers and gods, good conduct, austerity and non-aversion to liberation (Yogabindu).
A person born with the dharma of yogins, fit for instruction (YDS).

literal: yogin whose wheel is in motion

definitions.definition: A practitioner in whom the wheel of practice has begun to turn (YDS).

In Jainism the soul (jīva) as knower; each is distinct and eternal, of three conditions (outer, inner, supreme) (Samādhitantra 4); 'the self conquered by passions is saṃsāra, the self that conquers them is liberation' (YŚ 4.5).
The soul that takes the body and external things for itself (Samādhitantra 5).
The soul that discerns itself as distinct from the body — from right view onward (Samādhitantra 5).
In Jainism the soul in its perfected state — the embodied omniscient (arhat) and the bodiless Siddha; by the ultimate standpoint every soul's own nature (Paramātmaprakāśa; Yogasāra 22).
The soul seen by the pure standpoint as unbound, one, formless and made of knowledge and perception (Samayasāra 14, 38).
The object of self-experience and the refuge of right view.
The soul as pure knower, neither careless nor careful, beyond all states it knows (Samayasāra 6).
The soul abiding in its own knowing nature, as opposed to para-samaya, the soul identified with the non-self (Samayasāra 2).
Knowing the self as distinct from body, karma and passions; the cause of liberation (Samayasāra-kalaśa 131; Iṣṭopadeśa 50).
The central practice of the Adhyātma path: discerning the knower from all that is known.
The direct experience of one's own self, by which the samayasāra shines (Samayasāra-kalaśa 1); Hemacandra's 'established by experience' (YŚ 12.1).
The soul as consciousness; in the Samayasāra Nāṭaka the hero of the drama of self and non-self.
The self as consciousness and bliss (YŚ 10.1; Jñānasāra; the pen-name of the poet Cidānanda).
A member of the seventeenth-century Adhyātma movement.
A study circle of the Adhyātma movement meeting to read and discuss the Samayasāra and related texts.
The self-realised teacher marked by self-knowledge, equal vision, action only from past karma, unique speech and scriptural mastery (Ātmasiddhi 10).
One who seeks sect and opinion rather than the self (Ātmasiddhi).
One whose aim is the self alone, fit for the true teacher's instruction (Ātmasiddhi).
Śrīmad Rājacandra's six fundamentals: the soul exists, is eternal, is the doer, is the enjoyer, liberation exists, and there is a means (Ātmasiddhi 43).
The embodied omniscient who has destroyed the four destructive karmas; the first of the five supreme beings (arihanta 'destroyer of enemies' in popular etymology).

equivalents.note: Shared word; the Jain arhat is omniscient and will attain siddhahood, the Buddhist arahant has destroyed the āsavas — neither tradition equates the two.

definitions.definition: In Jainism a soul freed of all eight karmas, bodiless, abiding at the summit of the universe in infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy (TS 10.4–5).
An omniscient who establishes the fourfold community and teaches the path in a given age; twenty-four in each half-cycle.
One who has conquered attachment and aversion — the Tīrthaṅkara or any omniscient.
The passionless one, the true god for Jains (Ratnakaraṇḍa 5; Aṣṭaka 1; Vītarāgastotra).
In Jainism the head of an order, third of the five supreme beings, who receives the Sūrimantra at installation.
The monk who teaches the scriptures, fourth of the five supreme beings.
The five supreme beings — Arhat, Siddha, Ācārya, Upādhyāya, Sādhu — with 12, 8, 36, 25 and 27 qualities (108 in all).
One enlightened by an external cause without a teacher's instruction, contrasted with the one enlightened by another (buddhabodhita) (TS 10.9).
The divine hall built by the gods where the omniscient Tīrthaṅkara teaches all beings; the object of rūpastha meditation.
The Tīrthaṅkara's teaching-sound, understood by every being in its own language (Digambara: a sound without syllables emanating from his body).
In Jainism sound is a mode of matter (TS 5.24), not eternal; linguistic sound is formed from the 'language-class' of matter.
The four classes of Digambara literature: narratives (prathama), cosmology and karma (karaṇa), conduct (caraṇa), and substances (dravya) (Ratnakaraṇḍa 43–46).
Three follies obstructing right view: of the world (bathing in rivers for merit and the like), of gods (worshipping passionate deities for favours), and of false ascetics (Ratnakaraṇḍa).
Eight kinds of pride obstructing right view — in knowledge, honour, family, caste, power, wealth, austerity and body (Ratnakaraṇḍa).

The five-line Prakrit homage to the Arhats, Siddhas, Ācāryas, Upādhyāyas and all Sādhus, with (Śvetāmbara) a four-line cūlikā; held to be eternal, the essence of the fourteen Pūrvas, and destroyer of all evil.
The four-line appendix of the Namaskāra mantra declaring its power (eso paṃca-ṇamokkāro…).
The seed-syllable of the Arhat, central in word-based meditation (YŚ 8) and in the fire concentration (YŚ 7).
The five-syllable mantra formed from the initials of arhat, siddha (or aśarīra), ācārya, upādhyāya, sādhu (Dravyasaṃgraha 49 commentary).
In Jain explanation Oṃ is formed from the initials of the five supreme beings: a (arhat) + a (aśarīra, the Siddha) + ā (ācārya) + u (upādhyāya) + m (muni).
The secret mantra transmitted orally to a Śvetāmbara monk when he is installed as ācārya, practised in five sections (pīṭha) with presiding deities.

notes: Wording is secret and not recorded.

definitions.definition: A protective vidyā associated with Mahāvīra, given to Śvetāmbara monks at certain stages (low confidence on details).
A yantra and hymn centred on 'hrīṃ' with the five supreme beings and twenty-four Jinas, worshipped for protection.
The Śvetāmbara yantra of the nine padas (navapada), worshipped especially during the twice-yearly Olī.
Arhat, Siddha, Ācārya, Upādhyāya, Sādhu, right view, right knowledge, right conduct and austerity — the nine objects of Siddhacakra worship.
The attendant goddess (śāsana-devī, yakṣī) of Pārśvanātha, with Dharaṇendra; worshipped for protection and worldly aims, especially by Digambara bhaṭṭārakas and in Karnataka (Hombuja).
The nāga king and attendant yakṣa of Pārśvanātha, who sheltered him with his hoods during Kamaṭha's assault.
The yakṣa and yakṣī attendant on each Tīrthaṅkara, protecting the community; not objects of worship for liberation.
Attendant goddess of Candraprabha, subject of Indranandi's mantra manual.
A fast day with one meal of plain boiled grain without salt, oil, spices or milk, central to the Navapada Olī.
The chief Jain festival at the end of the rains-retreat season — eight days for Śvetāmbaras ending with forgiveness, ten days of the ten virtues (Daśalakṣaṇa) for Digambaras.
The lowest one-sensed beings, infinitely many sharing one body, filling the universe; the reservoir from which souls enter higher states.
Four kinds of distracting talk — about women, food, country and kings — a form of carelessness.
In Haribhadra's correlation the limb matching the mitrā view (YDS 16); in Jain terms the vows.
In Haribhadra's correlation the limb matching the tārā view (YDS 16).
In Haribhadra's correlation the limb of the balā view; Hemacandra lists the postures for meditation (paryaṅka, vīra, vajra, lotus, bhadra, daṇḍa, utkaṭikā, godohikā, kāyotsarga) (YŚ 4.124–134).

Described by Hemacandra and Śubhacandra (inhaling, holding, exhaling; the winds and their circles) but declared not a means to liberation because it torments the mind (YŚ 6.4–5); Haribhadra's dīprā view gives it an inner sense — expelling outer states and taking in inner ones.
In Haribhadra's correlation the limb of the sthirā view; in Hemacandra (YŚ 6) withdrawing the senses and mind from objects.
In Jainism (1) the limb of Haribhadra's parā view; (2) composure of the ascetic tended by others (sādhu-samādhi, TS 6.24); (3) peaceful death (samādhi-maraṇa).
